distributed-systems-architectural-styles.core: Architecture is a set of trade-offs: monoliths are simple, modular monoliths add enforced boundaries, microservices add autonomy at the cost of distribution, SOA taught us to avoid central buses, event-driven communication decouples in time, and processes are coordinated by orchestration or choreography.

first_principles.problem: Choosing architecture by fashion leads to unnecessary complexity or painful coupling.
truths: Boundaries matter more than deployment units.

analogy.title: Urban planning choices
analogy.story: One big building, a well-zoned campus or a city of independent districts, connected by roads or post.
analogy.breaks: Cities evolve over centuries; software architecture can evolve in years, if boundaries are clean.

example.title: Evolution path
flow: Year 2: modular monolith with enforced modules
Year 3: extract payments + search as services
Events between services; workflows for sagas

check.q: What's the recommended starting architecture for a small team with an unclear domain?
check.a: A (modular) monolith.

distributed-systems-time-and-clocks.core: Distributed systems have no global clock: physical clocks drift (NTP gives milliseconds, PTP microseconds), leap seconds and corrections make wall time jump, so durations need monotonic clocks. Ordering uses logical time (Lamport for causally consistent order, vector clocks to detect concurrency) or bounded-uncertainty hybrids like TrueTime and HLC.

first_principles.problem: Timestamp-based ordering silently produces wrong results across machines.

analogy.title: Coordinating a worldwide relay without a shared watch
analogy.story: Batons carry counters, watches are calibrated and you wait out the known error.
analogy.breaks: Relays have one baton; distributed systems have many concurrent messages.

example.title: Designing a replicated store
flow: Logs: NTP-synced wall time + offsets monitored

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Pick the right notion of time per job.

check.q: Which clock type detects concurrent events?
check.a: Vector clocks.

distributed-systems-control-theory.core: Control theory explains distributed-system behaviour: feedback loops measure and correct (negative feedback stabilises, positive feedback runs away), PID-style controllers balance responsiveness and stability, autoscalers need damping for delays and noise, thundering herds need jitter and coalescing, and backpressure keeps producers within consumers' capacity.

first_principles.problem: Controllers in production oscillate, overshoot or amplify failures.

analogy.title: Keeping a ship steady in waves
analogy.story: Measured, damped steering, avoiding overcorrection and keeping the bilge pumps ahead of leaks.
analogy.breaks: Ships face natural waves; distributed systems often create their own waves (retries, herds).

check.q: What does backpressure do?
check.a: Signals a producer to slow down when the consumer can't keep up.

distributed-systems-probabilistic-data-s.core: Probabilistic data structures answer membership (Bloom, Cuckoo), cardinality (HyperLogLog), frequency (Count-Min Sketch) and top-k questions with fixed, tiny memory and proven error bounds, using fast uniform hash functions. They power databases, caches, CDNs and analytics at scale.

first_principles.problem: Exact answers over massive data need impractical memory.

analogy.title: Statistical sampling for computers
analogy.story: Clever summaries give near-exact answers without storing everything.
analogy.breaks: Surveys sample people; sketches see every item but compress it.

example.title: Real-time analytics pipeline
flow: HLL counts daily uniques per country

check.q: Which structure would you use to count distinct users?
check.a: HyperLogLog.

distributed-systems-domain-driven-design.core: Domain-Driven Design closes the gap between business and code: a ubiquitous language shared with experts, bounded contexts that keep models focused, and tactical patterns (entities, value objects, aggregates as consistency boundaries, domain events, anti-corruption layers and repositories) that express the model cleanly.

first_principles.problem: Software built on misunderstood or tangled domain concepts becomes brittle and wrong.

analogy.title: Building a city with clear districts and local laws
analogy.story: Each district has its own rules and vocabulary, with border controls for trade.
analogy.breaks: Cities have fixed borders; contexts may be redrawn as understanding grows.

example.title: Insurance platform
flow: Contexts: Underwriting, Policy Admin, Claims, Billing

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Model the business, not the database.

check.q: What defines an aggregate's boundary?
check.a: The set of invariants that must be kept consistent together within one transaction.

distributed-systems-resiliency-patterns.core: Resiliency patterns assume failure and contain it: timeouts bound waiting, retries with backoff and jitter absorb transient errors safely, circuit breakers fail fast through closed/open/half-open states, bulkheads isolate resources, and fallbacks plus rate limiting keep services useful and protected under stress.

first_principles.problem: Partial failures cascade into total outages without defensive design.

analogy.title: A well-designed electrical system
analogy.story: Fuses, circuit breakers, separate circuits and backup generators.
analogy.breaks: Electrical faults are physical; software faults include slowness, which is harder to detect.

example.title: Resilient checkout
flow: One retry layer with jitter + idempotency keys
Fallback: queue order for later payment

check.q: Which pattern stops calling a failing dependency for a while?
check.a: The circuit breaker.

distributed-systems-consensus-algorithms.core: Consensus lets a group of unreliable nodes agree on an ordered log, acting as one reliable machine. FLP limits guaranteed liveness, so algorithms keep safety always and use timeouts for progress. Majority quorums intersect to prevent split-brain, Paxos pioneered the approach, Raft made it understandable (elections plus log replication), Zab powers ZooKeeper, and production needs careful timeouts, placement and membership changes.

first_principles.problem: Replicated systems diverge or split-brain without principled agreement.

analogy.title: A parliament keeping official records
analogy.story: Majority votes, elected speakers with terms, and minutes everyone must follow in order.
analogy.breaks: Parliaments meet in one room; nodes communicate over unreliable networks.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Consensus is the bedrock; operate it with care.

check.q: Which consensus algorithm does etcd use?
check.a: Raft.

distributed-systems-consistency-models.core: Consistency models define what replicated data looks like to clients: linearizability (a single real-time copy), sequential (one agreed order), causal (cause before effect, partition-available), eventual (converges eventually) and client-centric session guarantees for good UX. Stronger models cost latency and availability.

first_principles.problem: Without a chosen model, replicated systems surprise users with stale, reordered or lost data.

analogy.title: Different rules for different shared documents
analogy.story: Contracts need one signed copy; meeting notes can sync later; your own edits should always show.
analogy.breaks: Documents are few; systems handle millions of operations needing per-operation choices.

example.title: Social banking app
example.outcome: correct and fast where each matters.

check.q: Which model is the strongest that stays available during network partitions?
check.a: Causal consistency.

distributed-systems-distributed-transact.core: When data spans services, atomicity needs protocols: 2PC gives true atomicity but blocks on coordinator failure, 3PC isn't safe under partitions, sagas chain local transactions with compensations (orchestrated or choreographed), and TCC reserves then confirms or cancels. Idempotency and outboxes make all of them reliable.

first_principles.problem: Split databases leave business operations half-done on partial failure.

analogy.title: Planning a multi-vendor event
analogy.story: Book vendors with refundable deposits, confirm when everything's lined up, and have a cancellation plan.
analogy.breaks: Vendors negotiate; services follow coded protocols exactly.

example.title: E-commerce checkout
flow: Orchestrated saga: hold → capture payment (pivot) → ship → email

check.q: What's the main drawback of 2PC across services?
check.a: It blocks participants (holding locks) if the coordinator fails, hurting availability.

distributed-systems-formal-verification-.core: Formal verification with TLA+ specifies systems as state machines (Init, Next, invariants), often via friendlier PlusCal, and uses the TLC model checker to explore every interleaving in small configurations. It finds design bugs (lost updates, split-brain, deadlocks) that testing misses, before code exists.

first_principles.problem: Distributed designs fail in rare interleavings that tests never exercise.

analogy.title: Engineering blueprints checked by simulation
analogy.story: Every load and failure scenario simulated before construction.
analogy.breaks: Buildings follow blueprints exactly; code may diverge from specs.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Start small, on the riskiest design.

check.q: Which tool model-checks TLA+ specifications?
check.a: TLC.

distributed-systems-queueing-theory.core: Queueing theory explains latency: Little's law links in-flight work, throughput and latency; utilisation drives waits hyperbolically; Kingman's formula shows variability multiplies delay (the hockey stick); and the Universal Scalability Law shows contention and coherency limit how far adding nodes helps.

first_principles.problem: Capacity planning by averages produces terrible tail latency and wasted scaling.
truths: Scaling has diminishing or negative returns.

analogy.title: Managing a busy airport
analogy.story: Planes per hour, time at gates, runway busyness, irregular arrivals and the limits of adding runways.
analogy.breaks: Airports schedule slots; most systems face uncontrolled arrivals.

example.title: Capacity plan for an API
flow: λ = 3,000 rps, W = 50 ms → L = 150 in flight
USL fit sets max cluster size

check.q: What does Little's law relate?
check.a: Average items in the system, arrival rate and average time in the system (L = λW).

distributed-systems-metastable-failures.core: Metastable failures are self-sustaining bad states: a brief trigger tips a vulnerable system into overload, and feedback loops (retry storms, cache stampedes) keep it there. Prevent them with headroom, retry budgets, request coalescing and probabilistic early expiration, and escape them by shedding load and ramping back gradually.

first_principles.problem: Systems stay down long after the original cause is fixed.

analogy.title: A crowd crush that sustains itself
analogy.story: Pressure keeps building until entrances are closed and people are let out gradually.
analogy.breaks: Crowds are visible; system metastability can look like a normal outage.

example.title: Hardening a read-heavy service
flow: Game day: cache flush + recovery drill

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Design for recovery, not just peak.

check.q: Name two mechanisms that commonly sustain metastable failures.
check.a: Retry storms and cache stampedes.

distributed-systems-cell-based-architect.core: Cell-based architecture slices a system into independent full-stack cells serving subsets of customers behind a thin router. Blast radius shrinks to roughly 1/N, shuffle sharding makes full overlap between tenants astronomically unlikely, and heavy automation (templates, placement, migration, wave deploys) keeps operations manageable.

first_principles.problem: Shared layered architectures let one failure affect every customer.

analogy.title: A fleet of independent ships instead of one giant ship
analogy.story: If one ship has trouble, the rest of the fleet sails on.
analogy.breaks: Ships can rescue each other; cells shouldn't depend on each other.

example.title: Multi-tenant SaaS
flow: Thin router: DynamoDB mapping cached at edge

check.q: What is the role of the cell router?
check.a: To map each request's partition key (e.g. customer) to its cell with minimal logic.

distributed-systems-crdts.core: CRDTs let replicas update concurrently without coordination and always converge, because merges are commutative, associative and idempotent. LWW sets trade simplicity for clock reliance, OR-Sets give add-wins semantics with tags, G/PN-Counters count exactly, and state-, op- or delta-based variants trade bandwidth against delivery requirements.

first_principles.problem: Collaborative, offline and geo-replicated apps lose or conflict on concurrent edits.

analogy.title: A shared notebook with rules everyone follows when combining copies
analogy.story: No meetings needed; the rules guarantee everyone ends with the same notebook.
analogy.breaks: People might disagree with the result; CRDT rules may not match user intent in every case.

example.title: Collaborative whiteboard
flow: OR-Set of shapes, LWW registers for properties

check.q: Which CRDT set gives add-wins semantics without timestamps?
check.a: The OR-Set (Observed-Remove Set).

distributed-systems-leader-election-nuan.core: Leader election simplifies coordination but creates the danger of stale leaders: partitions and pauses mean a deposed node may keep acting. Use consensus-backed elections, leases with monotonic clocks and safety margins, and above all fencing tokens checked by resources to make zombie leaders harmless.

first_principles.problem: Multiple nodes believing they're leader corrupt data or duplicate work.
truths: Leaders can't detect their own staleness.

analogy.title: A rotating club captaincy with numbered armbands
analogy.story: Referees only accept instructions from the latest armband number.
analogy.breaks: Captains hand over armbands physically; leadership transfers happen without the old leader's knowledge.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Optimistic concurrency is a form of fencing.

check.q: What makes a zombie leader harmless?
check.a: Fencing tokens checked by resources, rejecting writes from older leadership terms.

distributed-systems-gossip-protocols.core: Gossip protocols spread information by random peer exchanges, reaching all nodes in O(log N) rounds with constant per-node load and no central point. SWIM adds scalable failure detection with indirect probes and suspicion, libraries like memberlist make it production-ready, and piggybacking makes dissemination nearly free.

first_principles.problem: Central coordination doesn't scale to thousands of nodes and becomes a single point of failure.

analogy.title: A village news network
analogy.story: News spreads by chats, absent neighbours are checked on, and messages ride along with daily visits.
analogy.breaks: Villages are small; gossip clusters scale to tens of thousands of nodes.

example.title: Service discovery cluster
flow: Servers use Raft for catalog consistency

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Gossip for membership, consensus for authoritative state.

check.q: What problem does SWIM solve compared with all-to-all heartbeats?
check.a: It detects failures with constant per-node load instead of O(N²) messages.

distributed-systems-distributed-locking.core: Distributed locks are leases: they expire to survive crashes, but expiry plus pauses and clock drift means two holders can overlap. Use simple Redis locks only for efficiency; Redlock still relies on timing and lacks fencing. For correctness, use consensus-backed locks (etcd, ZooKeeper) and pass their monotonic revisions as fencing tokens, or avoid locks with idempotency and partitioning.

first_principles.problem: Locks that seem exclusive allow overlapping holders under real-world failures.

analogy.title: Sharing dangerous equipment
analogy.story: Booking slots, timed keys and a logbook the machine itself checks before running.
analogy.breaks: Machines can lock physically; software resources must implement token checks.

check.q: Which systems provide correctness-grade distributed locks with fencing tokens?
check.a: Consensus stores like etcd (revisions) and ZooKeeper (zxids/sequence numbers).

distributed-systems-load-shedding.core: Load shedding keeps services useful when demand outpaces capacity faster than autoscaling can react: measure goodput (successful, on-time work) rather than raw throughput, shed by criticality so valuable requests survive, and use admission control with adaptive concurrency limits to reject cheaply at the door.

first_principles.problem: Overloaded services that try to serve everyone end up serving no one.

analogy.title: Emergency room triage plus a door policy
analogy.story: Serve the most urgent fully, turn away what can wait and never let the waiting room overflow.
analogy.breaks: ERs never turn away emergencies; systems decide by configured priority.

check.q: What is goodput?
check.a: The rate of requests completed successfully within their deadline.

distributed-systems-event-sourcing-cqrs.core: Event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event and derives state by replay, enabling audit, time travel and rebuildable projections. CQRS separates command handling from query-optimised read models fed by those events. Both add complexity, so use them in rich domains where history and divergent read needs justify it.

first_principles.problem: Overwrite-in-place databases lose history and force one model to serve conflicting needs.

analogy.title: Accounting ledgers with management reports
analogy.story: The ledger records every transaction; reports summarise it in different ways for different readers.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers close yearly; event streams live indefinitely.

example.title: Payments platform
flow: Projections: ledger, merchant dashboard, fraud features
Replay to rebuild after bug fixes

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: History as an asset, complexity as a cost.

example.outcome: auditable, flexible systems where it matters.

check.q: What does CQRS separate?
check.a: The model for handling commands (writes) from the models used for queries (reads).

distributed-systems-actor-model.core: The actor model handles concurrency by banning shared state: each actor owns its data, talks only through asynchronous messages, and processes one message at a time. Failures are contained and handled by supervisors that restart crashed actors, and runtimes range from explicit (Erlang, Akka) to virtual (Orleans).

first_principles.problem: Lock-based concurrent code deadlocks, races and is hard to scale across machines.

analogy.title: An office of clerks with in-trays and managers
analogy.story: Each clerk owns their desk, works through their tray in order, and managers replace clerks who break down.
analogy.breaks: Offices tolerate chatter; actors share nothing but messages.

example.title: Chat system
flow: Each chat room is an actor
Users send messages to room address
Crashed room restarts from persisted log

check.q: How does the actor model avoid locks?
check.a: Each piece of state has a single owner that processes messages serially, so nothing is accessed concurrently.

distributed-systems-merkle-trees.core: A Merkle tree hashes data in a hierarchy: leaves hash blocks, parents hash children, and one root commits to everything. That lets you prove membership with log-sized proofs, find differences between replicas by descending only mismatched branches, and build tamper-evident logs such as Git and blockchains.

first_principles.problem: Verifying or reconciling huge datasets over a network is too slow byte-by-byte.

analogy.title: Nested sealed envelopes
analogy.story: Each envelope's seal is made from the seals inside it; check the outer seal to trust everything within.
analogy.breaks: Envelopes can be steamed open; hash collisions are computationally infeasible.

example.title: Package registry log
flow: Every published package appended as leaf
Client gets inclusion proof on install

check.q: What do Merkle trees make logarithmic?
check.a: Proof size and the work to verify membership or locate differences, relative to the number of blocks.

distributed-systems-consistent-hashing.core: Consistent hashing places keys and nodes on the same hash ring so each key belongs to its clockwise successor. Membership changes then move only about 1/N of keys. Virtual nodes even out load and spread failover, and variants such as jump, rendezvous and Maglev hashing suit different needs.

first_principles.problem: Modulo hashing reshuffles nearly every key whenever a cluster grows or shrinks.
derivation: Place nodes and keys on a **ring**.

analogy.title: Bus stops on a loop road
analogy.story: Passengers take the next stop; adding a stop only affects those just before it.
analogy.breaks: Stops are planned; hashed nodes land randomly, hence vnodes.

example.title: Scaling a cache tier
flow: 10 memcached nodes with modulo: add 1 → ~91% miss
Switch to Ketama ring with 160 vnodes

check.q: What does consistent hashing guarantee on adding a node?
check.a: Only the keys on the new node's arc move, about 1/N of the total, all from one neighbour (or a few with vnodes).

distributed-systems-rate-limiting-algori.core: Rate limiting protects shared capacity by capping requests per client per unit of time. Fixed windows are simple but allow boundary bursts, sliding windows fix that, the leaky bucket shapes traffic into a steady outflow, and the token bucket allows bounded bursts while capping the average. Distributed limits need atomic shared state or approximate local counters.

first_principles.problem: Without limits, one client can exhaust capacity for everyone.
truths: Counting needs a clock and identity.

analogy.title: A bouncer with a clicker
analogy.story: Counts people in, keeps a steady pace or allows a group in if the room was empty, and tells others when to come back.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers bend rules; limiters don't.

example.title: API tiers
flow: Enforced in gateway via Redis Lua
Payment backend behind leaky bucket at 10/s

check.q: Why is the token bucket the common default for public APIs?
check.a: It caps the average rate while allowing the short bursts that normal client behaviour produces, without adding queueing latency.

distributed-systems-jepsen-testing.core: Jepsen verifies distributed-database consistency claims empirically: it runs concurrent workloads on a real cluster, injects partitions, crashes, pauses and clock faults, records every operation, and mathematically checks whether the history satisfies the promised model. Its findings show that guarantees must be verified under failure, not taken from marketing.

first_principles.problem: Consistency guarantees are claimed but rarely proven under real faults.

analogy.title: Independent crash-testing for databases
analogy.story: Not the manufacturer's brochure but a lab that smashes cars and publishes the footage.
analogy.breaks: Cars have standard tests; each DB needs workloads matched to its claims.

example.title: Adopting Jepsen thinking
flow: Read Jepsen report for chosen DB

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Guarantees verified before production finds out.

check.q: What three ingredients make up a Jepsen test?
check.a: A workload that records operation histories, a nemesis that injects faults, and a checker that verifies the history against a consistency model.
